analysis.one_liner: Phases out routine antibiotic use in food animals to keep human antibiotics working.
analysis.headline: Backed by 77 House Democrats and more than 400 health and consumer groups, the bill died without a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to withdraw approval for routine, non-medical uses of medically important antibiotics in cattle, pigs, and poultry within two years, unless drug makers could show the uses pose no risk to human health through antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics would still be allowed for sick animals and for genuine disease outbreaks on a farm, but not for growth promotion or blanket prevention dosed through feed and water. The bill's findings note that about 80 percent of antibiotics sold in the U.S. went to food animals, and that drug-resistant infections cause an estimated 23,000 American deaths a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who may need an antibiotic to work — patients facing surgery, chemotherapy, or ordinary infections — because cutting routine livestock dosing slows the spread of resistant bacteria. Sustainable livestock producers, who already raise animals without routine antibiotics, also gain a more level market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who might need a working antibiotic

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to withdraw approval of routine, non-medical (nontherapeutic) uses of medically important antibiotics in cattle, pigs, and poultry within two years unless the drug maker shows a reasonable certainty of no harm to human health from resistance caused by that use.

Protects the effectiveness of antibiotics that modern medicine depends on; the bill cites CDC estimates that resistant infections cause at least 2 million infections, 23,000 deaths, 8 million extra hospital days, and $20–35 billion in excess health costs each year, and notes that surgery, chemotherapy, and transplants rely on working antibiotics.

Still allows treatment of sick animals and targeted control of real disease outbreaks, but only where disease is present on the premises, for the shortest duration, and at the barn or pen level for the fewest animals possible — not blanket dosing of whole herds through feed and water.

Ends growth-promotion and feed-efficiency uses, the low-dose routine feeding that the bill's findings say accounted for the great majority of antibiotic tonnage going to food animals — about 80 percent of all antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Animal-drug manufacturers lose sales of routine feed antibiotics, and large livestock operations lose a cheap tool for growth promotion and blanket disease prevention. Any adjustment costs could show up modestly in meat prices, though the EU and Danish experience cited in the bill found antibiotic use fell after similar bans without cutting production.
analysis.who_pays_short: Animal-drug makers and large livestock operations

drawbacks.text: The two-year deadline is fast, and the burden falls on drug makers to prove a negative — that no harm to human health comes from resistance tied to the use — or lose the approval, which industry would call confiscatory.

Producers argued routine dosing controls disease in large herds and keeps meat cheap; the bill's own findings point the other way, noting the EU banned growth-promotion uses in 2006 and Danish data showed resistance fell without cutting production, but transitioning U.S. herds could still carry costs.

The FDA already had a voluntary program (Guidances 209 and 213) to phase out growth-promotion uses, and defenders of that approach said mandatory withdrawal was unnecessary; the bill's findings concede the voluntary policy still allowed routine disease prevention without proof that a disease was present.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and long-term: keeping a limited arsenal of life-saving drugs effective, with the bill's own findings documenting that 80 percent of U.S. antibiotics went to food animals and that resistant infections already kill an estimated 23,000 Americans a year. The costs fall on specific industries that profit from routine dosing, and the EU and Danish experience cited in the bill suggests livestock production can adjust without shrinking. The bill is aggressive — a two-year deadline and the burden on drug makers to prove a negative — and its strongest objection is that the FDA already had a voluntary phase-out underway; but the bill's findings show that voluntary policy still allowed routine preventive dosing without any evidence of disease, which is the loophole this bill closes.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on March 23, 2015, with 22 original cosponsors; it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Four days later it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Health; the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill finished with 77 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

Its findings cited FDA data that about 80 percent of antibacterial drugs sold in the U.S. in 2010 went to food animals, and CDC estimates that resistant infections cause at least 2 million infections and 23,000 deaths a year.
More than 400 organizations, including the American Medical Association and the Infectious Diseases Society of America, supported enactment, according to the bill's findings.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Animal-drug makers and large livestock operations kept the status quo: routine antibiotic dosing continued under the FDA's voluntary guidance, with no mandatory phase-out ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Animal-drug makers and industrial livestock producers

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 22 original cosponsors and delivered introductory remarks when it was introduced.

for.name: 77 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

for.name: Medical and public-health organizations
for.role: Endorsing groups including the American Medical Association and the Infectious Diseases Society of America
for.what_they_did: Supported enactment of legislation phasing out nontherapeutic antibiotic use in farm animals; the bill cites more than 400 supporting organizations.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee where the bill sat; no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill remained in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Animal-drug makers and large livestock industry groups
against.role: Stakeholders in routine livestock antibiotic use
against.what_they_did: Favored the FDA's voluntary guidance over a mandatory phase-out and opposed legislation requiring withdrawal of approved feed-antibiotic uses.

sides.party_line_note: All 77 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-chaired Energy and Commerce Committee never scheduled action, so the bill died without a vote.

industries.note: The bill forces FDA to pull approval of routine, non-medical uses of medically important antibiotics in food animals unless makers prove no resistance risk, eliminating a market the bill's findings put at roughly 80 percent of all antibiotics sold in the U.S.

Ends growth-promotion and blanket disease-prevention dosing; antibiotics would be limited to sick animals and genuine on-farm outbreaks, at pen or barn scale. The EU and Danish experience cited in the bill suggests production held up after similar bans.

Producers who already raise animals without routine antibiotics gain a level market instead of competing against cheap routine dosing; the National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition is listed among the bill's supporters.

Fewer resistant infections would cut the 8 million extra hospital days and $20–35 billion in annual excess costs the bill attributes to resistance — costs now borne by patients, insurers, and hospitals.
